title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Chapter 'De loco lunae ex eclipsibus lunaribus determinando' of an unpublished lunar-theory treatise. The aim is to use lunar eclipses to fix the Moon's true place in its orbit. At an eclipse the shadow centre lies on the ecliptic, opposite the Sun.

Notation: x is the shadow's (equivalently the anti-Sun's) longitude from the node at mid-eclipse. rho is the orbital inclination. m, n, k are the hourly motions of Sun, Moon and node.

In §13 Euler showed the following. At mid-eclipse (closest approach of Moon and shadow centre in relative motion), the Moon's orbital longitude, measured from the node, differs from the shadow's ecliptic longitude by a small equation of the form C·tan^2(rho/2)·sin 2x. The coefficient is C = (m+n+2k)/(n-m) = 1 + 2(m+k)/(n-m). It combines two pieces:
- the ordinary reduction to the ecliptic, tan^2(rho/2) sin 2x;
- the shift of mid-eclipse away from true opposition. The previous page gives this shift as d = 2(m+k)(n+k)/(g(n-m)^2) · sin 2x · tan^2(rho/2), carried over via the relative-motion ratio.

On this page Euler inserts mean tabular hourly motions: m = 147.833'', n = 1976.467'', k = 7.933''. These give m+n+2k = 2140.166 and n-m = 1828.633, so C = 1.17036, which he writes as 1 + 1/6 + 1/300 + 1/3000.

He then tabulates the 'aequatio' for argument (Sun minus node) of 0 to 10 degrees, i.e. the eclipse limits:
- subtract in signs 0 and VI;
- add for 20 to 30 degrees of signs V and XI, by the symmetry of sin 2x.
The entries are proportional to sin 2x with a maximum of 2'55'' at 10 degrees. Back-solving: 175'' = C·tan^2(rho/2)·206265''·sin 20° requires rho ≈ 5°16'–5°17'. That is the maximal (syzygy-node) inclination appropriate to eclipse seasons. The whole column (0'18'', 0'36'', ..., 1'29'', 2'04'', 2'38'', 2'55'') is reproduced to about 1''.

§27 is a sensitivity analysis. The true hourly motions differ from the mean ones by up to about 300'' (Moon) and 5'' (Sun). Since dC/dn < 0 and dC/dm > 0, Euler raises n by 300'' and lowers m by 5''. The numerator then grows by 295'' and the denominator by 305'', giving C ≈ 2435/2134 = 1.14105, a defect of 0.0293 ≈ 1/34. The maximal 2'55'' equation therefore falls by only about 5''. This is negligible given how poorly the mid-eclipse instant can be observed.

The next page contrasts this with the other formulae of the chapter. There n does not enter numerator and denominator with equal weight, so true hourly motions are required. That motivates the following chapter on true motions, nodes and inclination, using the 1722 eclipse.
errors: With unrounded values the perturbed ratio is 2435.167/2133.633 = 1.14132, not 2435/2134 = 1.14105. The resulting defect is about 0.0290 rather than 0.02931. 1/34 = 0.0294 is only approximate.
The reduction of the 175'' maximum is actually 175 × 0.0293/1.170 ≈ 4.4'', which Euler rounds to 5''.

The perturbation chosen (n up, m down) is the extreme in one direction only. The opposite choice (n down 300'', m up 5'') gives C = 1845.2/1523.6 ≈ 1.211. That deviation is +0.041, about 6'' at 10°, which is larger in absolute value. So 'ut discrimen fiat maximum' is not strictly true, though the conclusion (a negligible effect) stands.
Variation of the node's hourly motion k is ignored in the error estimate; its effect is negligible.

ideas.what: Equation reducing the shadow's ecliptic longitude to the Moon's orbital longitude at mid-eclipse, with coefficient (m+n+2k)/(n-m) = 1 + 2(m+k)/(n-m). This combines the reduction to the ecliptic with the mid-eclipse–opposition offset in relative motion.
ideas.modern_name: Reduction to the ecliptic plus the correction from opposition to the instant of greatest eclipse (relative-orbit geometry)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th-century eclipse computation (e.g. Mayer, Lalande, Cassini tables); classical
ideas.where_published: Only in this posthumous text (E838, Opera postuma II, 1862) as far as known; Euler's lunar theories E187/E418 treat eclipses differently

ideas.what: Numerical table of this equation for Sun–node distances 0 to 10°, implicitly using inclination ≈ 5°16'–5°17'
Sensitivity analysis showing the coefficient is insensitive to errors in n because n enters numerator and denominator alike
ideas.modern_name: First-order error/sensitivity analysis of a ratio
ideas.usually_credited_to: Common practice; error analysis later formalized by Cotes, Simpson, Lambert, Gauss

deep.surprise_reason: Routine numerical application: mean motions are plugged into a previously derived coefficient, a small eclipse table is produced, and a correct but slightly one-sided sensitivity check follows. It is historically mildly interesting as evidence of Euler's practical eclipse-reduction procedure, implying i ≈ 5°17', but contains nothing that a specialist would find new.
